venerable

VEN-er-uh-bul -- shares a root with 'venerate,' meaning to regard with deep respect. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Venerable is worthy of great respect because of age, wisdom, or long service.

The venerable judge had presided over the county's most important trials for three decades.

Example

A retired general, now in his nineties, is invited to every graduation ceremony so cadets can hear firsthand what decades of service and wisdom sound like.

That deep respect earned through age and long service is exactly what venerable describes. Unlike 'old,' which is neutral about age alone, venerable specifically implies respect has been earned.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

distinguished: Distinguished means successful and respected for achievements, especially within a particular field, at any age. Venerable is respect of a different flavor: it is earned over a long lifetime of service and wisdom, which is why a brilliant newcomer cannot yet be venerable.

respected: Respected simply means held in high regard by others, for any good reason at all. Venerable is a narrower honor: it says the respect has been earned specifically through great age, deep wisdom, or many years of service.

time-honored: Time-honored describes customs, methods, and traditions respected because they have lasted for generations. Venerable does the same work for people and institutions: a venerable judge or university has earned deep respect through its own long life of service.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

shady: of doubtful honesty or reputation

disgraced: having lost the respect of others due to a shameful act

Where it sits · how deep the respect runs — esteemed → venerable → revered

esteemed vs. venerable: Esteemed is a bit milder than venerable -- esteemed simply means well-respected, while venerable adds the specific sense that this respect comes from long service or advanced age.

revered vs. venerable: Revered can feel even stronger than venerable: venerable implies earned respect through age and wisdom, while revered suggests an almost reverent, near-worshipful admiration.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — -vener-

root — -vener-: to worship, respect deeply (Latin (venerari))

suffix — -able

suffix — -able: able to be, worthy of being (Latin (-abilis))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin venerari meant 'to worship, regard with deep respect,' and adding -able ('worthy of being') gives 'worthy of being deeply respected.' The same root gives us venerate.

Use the root in a new word: venerate

Use the root in a new word: venerate: The small village continues to venerate the founder who built its first schoolhouse two centuries ago.
